questions.question: What is the Factory design pattern?
questions.title: Factory pattern — object creation without new
questions.direct_answer: A factory moves a construction decision behind a method or object so callers depend on the product contract rather than construction details. The factory still uses constructors or another creation mechanism internally. It is useful when the concrete type varies, setup is complex, or lifecycle belongs to a separate component. Adding a product may still require updating registration or selection logic.

sections.title: Factory Pattern Overview
sections.content:
A **factory** separates *using* an object from deciding how to construct it. A caller asks for a product contract such as `PaymentProcessor`, and a factory chooses and builds a concrete implementation.

The pattern does not eliminate `new`; it moves construction to a place that owns that responsibility. This can centralize configuration, validate a requested type, and keep callers independent of concrete constructors. The selection mechanism still has to know how products are registered or chosen, so adding a new product is not automatically a zero-change operation everywhere.

Use a factory when there is a real construction decision or lifecycle. Direct construction or ordinary dependency injection is clearer for a simple stable dependency.

sections.title: Without Factory — caller hardcodes concrete classes
With Factory — creation centralized behind an interface
Factory Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Product interface|~What callers depend on|Payment|hides concrete classes|swappable implementations
blue|Factory method|~Picks the type|create(type)|reads runtime data|returns the interface
emerald|Decoupling|~The real benefit|caller -> interface only|no new in client|Open/Closed Principle
violet|Three flavors|~Know the names|Simple Factory (static)|Factory Method (subclass)|Abstract Factory (family)

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling any object-returning method a factory.** `getUserById()` is a lookup, not a factory. Factory means choosing a concrete *type* behind an interface.
- **Using Factory for everything**, even simple value objects/DTOs — that's needless indirection. `new OrderItem(id, qty)` is fine.
- **Returning the concrete type** from the factory — return the interface, or callers stay coupled.
- **Missing the 'why'** — the value is adding types without editing client code (OCP), not just 'creating objects'.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A factory owns a construction decision and returns a product contract
- Constructors still run inside the factory or container
- Callers avoid depending on concrete setup details
- New products may require registration or selection changes
- Direct construction is clearer when no creation variation exists

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A factory moves object-construction decisions behind a method or component. The caller asks for a product interface, such as `PaymentProcessor`, and does not need to know the selected implementation's constructor or setup steps. The factory still creates the object internally; it does not remove `new`. This helps when the concrete type depends on input or configuration, or when creation has validation and resource setup. Adding a product may still require updating a registry or selection rule, so I do not claim automatic Open/Closed compliance. For a simple stable object, direct construction or normal dependency injection is easier to follow.

questions.question: When should you use the Factory pattern?
questions.title: When to use Factory pattern — appropriate use cases
questions.direct_answer: Reach for Factory when the **concrete type depends on runtime data** (pick a processor by country), when **creation is complex** (pools, timeouts, SSL), or when you want to **add types without editing callers** (OCP). Skip it for simple, stable objects — wrapping a DTO in a factory is needless indirection that violates **YAGNI**.

sections.title: Deciding When to Use Factory Pattern
sections.content:
Factory is a tool, not a default. Introduce it when the benefit beats the cost of extra indirection. Three signals say yes:

- **Runtime type selection** — the concrete class depends on user input, config, or environment (email vs SMS vs push by stored preference).
- **Complex creation** — instantiation needs multiple steps or resources (a `DataSource` with pool, timeouts, SSL).
- **Open/Closed** — you expect to add types often and want to do it by writing new classes, not editing callers.

The cost: indirection. You can't read `factory.create()` and instantly know the type. So for stable, simple objects, prefer `new`.

sections.title: Over-applied — factory for a trivial DTO (don't)
Justified — runtime selection of a real implementation
Factory: Use It or Skip It
sections.content:
amber|Use when|~Runtime type varies|processor by country|channel by preference|tenant by config
blue|Use when|~Creation is complex|pools + timeouts + SSL|multi-step setup|hide the mess
emerald|Skip when|~Stable + simple|DTOs, value objects|records|just use new
violet|Guardrail|~YAGNI|don't pre-abstract|wait for real pain|then refactor

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Factory everywhere.** Wrapping every `new` in a factory, even DTOs, adds indirection and hurts readability.
- **Introducing it too early.** Follow YAGNI — wait for duplicated creation code or real type variation before refactoring.
- **Confusing Factory with Service Locator.** Pulling beans from the context inside a 'factory' is the Service Locator anti-pattern; prefer DI to wire dependencies.
- **Hiding business logic in the factory.** A factory should create and wire, not run operations.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Runtime type selection** is the strongest signal to use Factory.
- **Complex creation** (resources, multi-step config) justifies it too.
- **Open/Closed** — add types without editing callers.
- **Cost is indirection** — harder to trace the concrete type.
- **YAGNI** — don't pre-abstract; refactor when pain appears.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: You use Factory when the exact class you need depends on runtime data. For example, in a notification service the user can choose email, SMS, or push, and that preference lives in the database. You can't hardcode new EmailNotifier everywhere, because tomorrow the same user might switch to SMS. A factory lets you pass the preference and get back the right notifier. The second reason is complex creation. Say you're building a database connection that needs a pool, timeout settings, SSL config, and credentials. Doing that inline every time is repetitive and error-prone, so a factory hides it behind a single create method. The third reason is the Open Closed Principle: when you add a new payment method like cryptocurrency, you add a class and a case in the factory, and the order service that calls the interface never changes. But there's a real trade-off — Factory adds indirection. When you see a PaymentProcessor variable, you can't tell at a glance whether it's Stripe or PayPal without tracing the factory. So I don't use Factory for simple objects. If I'm creating a DTO like new UserDto with an id and name, I just use new — a factory there is pure overhead. The rule of thumb is: use Factory when the type varies at runtime or creation is complex, and otherwise keep it simple. Two mistakes freshers make are using Factory everywhere because they read it's a best practice, and introducing it too early before there's any real variation. I'd follow YAGNI — wait until I actually feel the pain of hardcoded types or duplicated creation code, then refactor to a factory.

questions.question: How do you implement a Factory Method pattern in Java?
questions.title: Implementing Factory Method in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define an **abstract creator** with an abstract factory method returning an interface, plus a **template method** that uses it. Each **concrete subclass** overrides the factory method to return a specific product. The parent owns the workflow and depends only on the interface; subclasses supply the type. Adding a type = adding a subclass, not editing the parent.

sections.title: Implementing Factory Method Pattern
sections.content:
Factory Method is built on **inheritance and polymorphism**. Three layers:

1. An **abstract creator** declaring an abstract factory method that returns an interface.
2. A **template method** in the parent that calls the factory method and does the shared work.
3. **Concrete creators** that override the factory method to return a specific implementation.

The parent defines the workflow without knowing the exact types; subclasses provide them. That's the **Dependency Inversion Principle** — the high-level workflow depends on an abstraction, and subclasses plug in the concrete piece. Like a franchise: HQ defines how to make a burger (template), each branch decides the patty (factory method).

sections.title: Build It Step by Step
sections.content:
| Step | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define the product interface (`ReportGenerator`) | callers depend on abstraction |
| 2 | Abstract creator with `abstract createGenerator()` | the factory method |
| 3 | Template method `export()` calls `createGenerator()` | shared workflow, type-agnostic |
| 4 | `PdfReportService` overrides to return PDF generator | concrete creator |
| 5 | Add `ExcelReportService` later | new subclass, parent untouched (OCP) |

sections.title: Simple Factory — one static switch (not Factory Method)
Factory Method — subclasses override the creation method
Factory Method's Three Layers
sections.content:
amber|Product interface|~What's created|ReportGenerator|hides concrete types|callers depend on it
blue|Abstract creator|~Owns the workflow|abstract createGenerator|template method uses it|depends on abstraction
emerald|Concrete creators|~Supply the type|PdfReportService|override the method|add type = add subclass
violet|Principle|~Why it's GoF|inversion of control|parent calls subclass hook|follows OCP + DIP

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing it with Simple Factory.** A static helper isn't Factory Method — that needs inheritance and an overridden method.
- **No template method.** Overriding the factory method but having no parent method that *uses* it loses the inversion of control that gives the pattern its power.
- **Returning a concrete type** from the factory method — return the interface so subclasses can plug in any implementation.
- **Over-engineering** — for two types with no shared workflow, Simple Factory is plenty.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Abstract creator** declares the abstract factory method (returns an interface).
- **Template method** in the parent calls it and runs the shared workflow.
- **Concrete creators** override the factory method to supply the type.
- **Inheritance + polymorphism** — that's what makes it the GoF pattern.
- **OCP** — add a type by adding a subclass, not editing the parent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Factory Method is implemented with inheritance. You start with an abstract creator class that has an abstract factory method returning an interface type. Then you write a template method in the parent that calls the factory method to get an object and does the shared work with it — and crucially, the parent depends only on the interface, not any concrete class. Finally, you write subclasses that override the factory method to return specific implementations. The structure means the parent owns the workflow without knowing the exact types, and subclasses supply the types. Let me make it concrete with a report service. You define an abstract ReportService with an abstract method createGenerator that returns a ReportGenerator interface. Then you write an export method in the parent that calls createGenerator, then calls generate on whatever it gets back. The parent doesn't know if it's a PDF or Excel generator. Now you create subclasses, PdfReportService and ExcelReportService, and each overrides createGenerator to return its specific generator. The export method is identical for both, but it produces different reports because the factory method is overridden. The mistake freshers make is confusing this with Simple Factory. Factory Method needs inheritance and an overridden method — a static helper is Simple Factory. The other mistake is having no template method; if you override the creation method but nothing in the parent actually calls it, you've lost the whole benefit. The key difference to call out is this: with Simple Factory you edit an existing switch to add a type, but with Factory Method you add a new subclass and never touch existing code. That's why Factory Method is the Gang of Four pattern — it follows Open Closed and inverts control.

questions.question: What are the drawbacks of overusing the Factory pattern?
questions.title: Drawbacks of overusing Factory
questions.direct_answer: Overusing factories adds indirection, extra types, configuration, and another place to trace failures. It can hide a simple concrete dependency behind an abstraction that never varies. Plain construction is often clearer for a stable local object; the reason is readability and ownership, not a guaranteed performance advantage.

sections.title: Drawbacks of Factory Pattern Overuse
sections.content:
Factory isn't free. **Indirection**: `var s = factory.create()` hides the concrete type — you must trace the factory to know what you got, versus the instant clarity of `new OrderService()`. **Class proliferation**: Factory Method especially adds a creator subclass per product, so a handful of types can balloon into dozens of tiny classes. **Premature abstraction**: introducing Factory before you have multiple types or complex creation violates **YAGNI** and makes the code harder for the next reader.

Code is read far more than written. If teammates spend minutes tracing factory hierarchies to learn what object is created, that's waste. Use Factory when the flexibility justifies the cost — not by default.

sections.title: Over-engineered — factory + subclass for a fixed type
Right-sized — just use new until variation appears
Factory: Benefits vs Costs
sections.content: **Benefit — flexibility:** swap implementations without changing callers. **Cost — cognitive load:** readers must trace factory methods to know the type. **Benefit — testability:** inject a test factory returning mocks. **Cost — class explosion:** Factory Method needs a creator per product. **Benefit — Open/Closed:** add types by adding classes. **Cost — overkill for stable types:** for a fixed set (HTTP methods, weekdays) an enum or `new` is clearer. **Bottom line:** Factory trades simplicity for flexibility — pay only when the flexibility is real.

sections.title: Signs You've Overused Factory
sections.content:
amber|Indirection|~Hidden type|factory.create()|trace to know what|new is instant
blue|Class explosion|~Too many files|creator per product|tiny one-method classes|navigation cost
emerald|Premature|~YAGNI broken|added 'just in case'|one type only|no real variation
violet|Fix|~Right-size it|start with new|refactor on real pain|name the problem first

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating Factory as always better than `new`.** It's a trade-off; `new` is clearer for stable, simple objects.
- **Ignoring the debugging cost.** 'What type is this?' answered with 'it depends on the factory' is a smell.
- **Premature abstraction.** Adding Factory 'in case we need flexibility later' violates YAGNI — refactor when pain is real.
- **One product, full factory.** A factory with a single implementation is over-engineering.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Indirection cost** — Factory hides the concrete type, slowing reading/debugging.
- **Class proliferation** — Factory Method adds a creator per product.
- **YAGNI** — don't pre-abstract before multiple types or complex creation exist.
- **`new` is better** for DTOs, value objects, immutable records.
- **One-product factory** = over-engineering signal.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A factory has a cost: the reader must follow another method, registry, or creator hierarchy to discover what is built and why. It can also add types and configuration that provide no value when a dependency is simple and stable. I use a factory when concrete selection, complex setup, or lifecycle is a real responsibility. Otherwise a constructor or direct dependency injection is clearer. I do not justify that choice with a universal speed claim; object cost depends on the actual implementation, while the main trade-off here is design clarity and change ownership.

questions.question: How does the Factory pattern improve testability of Java code?
questions.title: Factory pattern and testability
questions.direct_answer: A factory can improve testability when the code under test must create a product during an operation: inject a factory interface and have the test return a controlled fake product. A static or internally constructed factory does not provide that seam by itself. If the dependency can simply be injected as an object, direct dependency injection is usually simpler than adding a factory.

sections.title: Factory Pattern and Testability
sections.content:
A factory creates a useful test seam only when it is supplied from outside the class under test. Production can provide a factory that builds real products, while a test provides one that returns a controlled fake.

This matters when creation is part of the behavior—for example, opening a client for a tenant selected at runtime. If the service always uses one collaborator, inject that collaborator directly instead of adding an unnecessary factory.

Calling a static factory or constructing the factory inside the method can leave the same hard dependency as calling a constructor. Testability comes from substitutable ownership, not from the word “Factory.”

sections.title: Untestable — new() hardcoded inside the method
Testable — inject the factory, swap it in tests
Factory as a Testing Seam
sections.content:
amber|The seam|~Control point|injected factory|swap real vs fake|production code unchanged
blue|Inject it|~Not new inside|constructor param|test passes a fake|isolation achieved
emerald|Avoid static|~Can't override|use instance/interface|or it can't be swapped|key gotcha
violet|Where it shines|~Beyond @MockBean|objects made per call|dynamic creation|DI alone can't help

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Static factory methods.** They can't be overridden or injected — use instance methods or a factory interface.
- **Missing the injection point.** If you `new RealFactory()` inside the service, you're back to a hard dependency. Inject the factory.
- **Business logic in the factory.** Keep factories to creation/wiring, or they become hard to test themselves.
- **Fake objects instead of real mocks.** Use a mocking framework (Mockito) when you need to verify interactions.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Inject a factory contract when runtime creation is genuinely part of the behavior
- Tests can make that factory return a fake or controlled product
- A static or internally constructed factory is not automatically substitutable
- Directly inject a stable collaborator when no creation decision is needed
- Keep lifecycle and cleanup behavior explicit in both production and test factories

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A factory improves testability when a method genuinely needs to create one of several products at runtime and the factory is injected through a contract. The production factory can build a real client, while the test factory returns a controlled fake, so the service behavior is isolated. Simply renaming a static creation method as a factory does not create that seam, because the class still owns a hard dependency. If the service always uses one repository or client, I inject that object directly; adding a factory would only add indirection. The value comes from external, substitutable ownership of a real creation decision.

questions.question: What is the difference between Simple Factory and Factory Method pattern?
questions.title: Simple Factory vs Factory Method pattern
questions.direct_answer: A Simple Factory is a common name for a function or object that selects and creates products, often from a switch or registry; it is not one of the named GoF patterns. Factory Method is the GoF pattern in which a creator defines a creation method and subclasses can override which product it supplies. Neither form automatically satisfies the Open/Closed Principle: selection, registration, and client construction still need design.

sections.title: Simple Factory vs Factory Method
sections.content:
A **Simple Factory** centralizes selection in one function or object. It might use a switch over a supported type or a registry of product suppliers. It is a useful idiom but not a separately named Gang of Four pattern.

**Factory Method** is a GoF pattern in which a creator exposes a factory method and subclasses decide the concrete product returned. The creator may use that product in a larger workflow. This trades a central switch for a creator hierarchy.

The difference is the extension mechanism, not “bad versus good.” A switch may be the clearest closed set. A registry can make a simple factory extensible. Factory Method adds subclasses and still requires callers or configuration to choose a concrete creator.

sections.title: Simple Factory vs Factory Method
sections.content:
| Aspect | Simple Factory | Factory Method (GoF) |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | One class, static method | Abstract creator + subclasses |
| GoF pattern? | No — an idiom | Yes — formal pattern |
| Open/Closed | Violates (edit the switch) | Follows (add a subclass) |
| Mechanism | `switch`/`if` | Overridden abstract method |
| Complexity | Low | Higher (inheritance) |
| Best for | Small, stable type set | Extensible systems, frameworks |

sections.title: Simple Factory — adding a type edits the switch
Factory Method — adding a type adds a subclass
Pick the Right One
sections.content:
amber|Simple Factory|~Informal idiom|static method + switch|easy to read|edits to add a type
blue|Factory Method|~GoF pattern|abstract creator + subclasses|inheritance based|extend to add a type
emerald|OCP angle|~The deciding factor|Simple violates|Factory Method follows|fewer regressions
violet|Progression|~Real teams|start Simple|refactor when extensibility matters|don't over-engineer early

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Simple Factory a GoF pattern.** It isn't — it's a precursor idiom the book only mentions.
- **Missing the OCP violation.** Every new type edits the Simple Factory switch; Factory Method avoids that with subclasses.
- **Over-applying Factory Method.** For a small stable type set, a static helper is fine; inheritance is overkill.
- **Thinking they're unrelated.** Simple Factory is usually the first step you later refactor into Factory Method.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Simple Factory centralizes selection in a function, class, switch, or registry
- It is a common idiom, not a separately named GoF pattern
- Factory Method lets creator subclasses override product creation
- Neither approach removes product registration or creator selection
- Choose the smaller extension mechanism that fits the expected change

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A Simple Factory is a common name for one function or object that chooses and creates a product, often with a switch or a registry. It is useful but is not one of the named GoF patterns. Factory Method is the GoF pattern where a creator defines a creation method and subclasses override which product it returns, often while the parent owns a larger workflow. The trade-off is central selection versus a creator class hierarchy. I would not say a simple factory always violates Open/Closed or Factory Method guarantees it: a registry can extend a simple factory, and some code still chooses the concrete creator. I select the simplest mechanism for the expected change.

questions.question: How does Spring use the Factory pattern?
questions.title: Factory pattern in Spring — ApplicationContext as a factory
questions.direct_answer: Spring's container performs factory responsibilities: `BeanFactory` and `ApplicationContext` locate and create bean definitions, resolve dependencies, and manage lifecycle. Most application code receives beans through injection rather than calling the container as a service locator. `FactoryBean<T>` is Spring's explicit extension point for custom object creation; an `@Bean` method is another container-managed creation recipe.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `BeanFactory` and `ApplicationContext` own bean lookup, creation, dependencies, scope, and lifecycle
- Application code normally receives beans through constructor injection
- Repeated `getBean()` calls in business code hide dependencies like a service locator
- `FactoryBean<T>` is Spring's extension point for custom product creation
- `@Bean` methods are container-managed creation recipes

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring's IoC container has factory responsibilities. `BeanFactory` and `ApplicationContext` read bean definitions, create the selected implementation, resolve dependencies, and manage scope and lifecycle. In normal application code I use constructor injection rather than calling `getBean`, because direct container lookup hides dependencies and behaves like a service locator. When construction itself is special, Spring provides `FactoryBean<T>`, whose `getObject()` supplies the product, and `@Bean` methods provide container-managed creation recipes. These ideas are factory-like, though I would not label every Spring mechanism as an exact textbook Factory Method implementation.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Spring's IoC container separates application code from bean construction. `BeanFactory` is the core bean-access contract, while `ApplicationContext` adds broader application services. Bean definitions and configuration tell the container which type to create, how to resolve its dependencies, and which lifecycle and scope rules apply.

Application classes normally use constructor injection. Calling `applicationContext.getBean(...)` throughout business code turns the container into a service locator and hides dependencies.

For special construction, a `FactoryBean<T>` is itself a managed bean whose `getObject()` supplies another object. An `@Bean` method also acts as a configuration recipe invoked by the container. These mechanisms have factory-like roles, but not every Spring creation feature is a literal textbook GoF Factory Method implementation.

sections.title: Spring Factory Pattern Example
How the Container Acts as a Factory
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Your code
getBean or @Autowired"] --> B["ApplicationContext
(extends BeanFactory)"] B --> C{"Bean exists
in scope?"} C -->|"Yes (singleton)"| D["Return cached instance"] C -->|"No"| E["Read bean definition
(@Bean / @Component)"] E --> F["Create instance
+ inject dependencies"] F --> G["Wrap in proxy if needed
(@Transactional, @Async)"] G --> H["Return fully wired bean"] D --> H ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing `BeanFactory` exists.** `ApplicationContext` extends it; `BeanFactory` is the actual factory interface.
- **Thinking `@Bean` is magic.** It's a factory method — Spring calls it, and you control the creation logic inside.
- **Calling `new` inside beans.** `new UserRepository()` bypasses the container, so Spring can't inject or manage it.
- **Ignoring scope.** Singleton vs prototype is the factory deciding whether to cache and reuse or create fresh.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Reach for Factory when the **concrete type depends on runtime data** (pick a processor by country), when **creation is complex** (pools, timeouts, SSL), or when you want to **add types without editing callers** (OCP). Skip it for simple, stable objects — wrapping a DTO in a factory is needless indirection that violates **YAGNI**.

questions.question: What is the Abstract Factory pattern?
questions.title: Abstract Factory — factory of factories
questions.direct_answer: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a related set of product types without exposing their concrete classes. A concrete factory supplies one variant of the family, such as Windows buttons and dialogs. It encourages compatible products to be selected together, but consistency still depends on the factory implementation and on not mixing products from other creation paths.

sections.title: Abstract Factory Pattern Explained
sections.content:
**Abstract Factory** creates **families of related objects** that must be used together and stay consistent — a step beyond Factory Method's single product.

Picture a UI framework on Windows and macOS. You need `Button`, `TextField`, and `ScrollBar`, but the platforms differ. Mixing a Windows button with a macOS text field looks broken. Abstract Factory prevents that: define a `GUIFactory` with `createButton()`, `createTextField()`, `createScrollBar()`, then implement `WindowsGUIFactory` and `MacGUIFactory`, each returning the matching set. The client depends only on `GUIFactory`, so switching the whole family is one line. Like a furniture collection — buy 'Modern' and you get matching Modern chairs and tables, never a Victorian chair by accident.

sections.title: Without Abstract Factory — easy to mismatch a family
With Abstract Factory — one family, guaranteed consistent
Abstract Factory at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Product family|~Related objects|Button + TextField + ScrollBar|must match|used together
blue|Abstract factory|~One interface|many create methods|one per product|client depends on it
emerald|Concrete factories|~Per family|WindowsGUIFactory|MacGUIFactory|returns matching set
violet|vs Factory Method|~The key word: family|Method = one product|Abstract = a suite|switch all in one line

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing it with Factory Method.** The tell is 'family' — multiple related products that must match means Abstract Factory.
- **Grouping unrelated objects.** Don't put `createUserRepository` and `createEmailValidator` in one factory just because they're nearby — they aren't a family.
- **Missing the consistency guarantee.** The whole point is preventing mix-and-match across families.
- **Using it for a single product.** That's Factory Method or Simple Factory.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Abstract Factory creates a family** of related objects that stay consistent.
- **One factory interface, many create methods** (one per product).
- **Concrete factories** each return a matching set (Windows vs Mac).
- **Consistency guarantee** — no mixing incompatible parts.
- **Vs Factory Method** — one product vs a whole family.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Abstract Factory is a pattern for creating families of related objects that must work together and stay consistent. The classic example is a UI toolkit. Imagine an app that runs on Windows and macOS. You need buttons, text fields, and scroll bars, but the Windows versions look different from the macOS versions. If developers can mix and match — a Windows button with a macOS text field — the interface looks broken. Abstract Factory prevents that. You define a GUIFactory interface with methods like createButton, createTextField, and createScrollBar. Then you implement two concrete factories, WindowsGUIFactory and MacGUIFactory, and each returns the matching set. The client code depends only on the GUIFactory interface, so you can switch the entire family by changing one line — which factory you instantiate. If the user is on Windows, you use WindowsGUIFactory and everything is Windows style; on macOS you swap to MacGUIFactory and everything matches. The key difference from Factory Method is that Factory Method creates one product, while Abstract Factory creates several related products. A backend example is JDBC: a driver creates a matching Connection, Statement, and ResultSet, all from the same vendor family, so swapping the driver gives you a consistent set for the new database. The mistake freshers make is confusing Abstract Factory with Factory Method. The giveaway is the word family — if you're creating multiple related objects that belong together and must stay consistent, it's Abstract Factory. Another mistake is grouping unrelated objects into one factory just because they're created in the same place. Use Abstract Factory only when consistency across the family actually matters.
